ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The study was performed according to the Declaration of Helsinki and its revisions, approved by the Swedish Ethical Review Authorities (original approval on date 2023-01-30, registration number 2022-06042-01, and amendment 2025-02584-02) and registered at ClinicalTrials.gov under ID: NCT05801042 (submission date 2023-02-10).

Participants of both sexes were recruited through local advertisement, screened at the study site and included if 60-80 years of age, body mass index 18.5-31.9 kg/m 2, willing to abstain from regular consumption of probiotic supplements or food products containing probiotic bacteria (including fermented food/beverages) and supplements/medications known to alter gastrointestinal function or inflammatory status, and self-reported healthy (e.g. lacking a metabolic, gastrointestinal, psychiatric, neurodegenerative diagnosis).

Participants were phenotypically characterised (and intervention effects were assessed 20 ) by researcher-administered tests (Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) 21 ), self-administered questionnaires assessing mental health and sleep quality (Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) 22, Perceived Stress Scale (PSS) 23, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) 24, Gastrointestinal Symptom Rating Scale (GSRS) 25 ) and blood markers (high sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP), Supplementary Information 1).
table.formatted: Participants were phenotypically characterised (and intervention effects were assessed <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20</ref> ) by researcher-administered tests (Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21</ref> ), self-administered questionnaires assessing mental health and sleep quality (Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22</ref> , Perceived Stress Scale (PSS) <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23</ref> , Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">24</ref> , Gastrointestinal Symptom Rating Scale (GSRS) <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25</ref> ) and blood markers (high sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP), Supplementary Information 1).

table.text: Block (size three and six) randomisation was performed, and participants were stratified by sex and age (born 1954 or later, born 1953 or earlier).
Participants were instructed to consume the study product daily, together with breakfast, dissolved in 200 ml of cold or room temperature water or milk.
Participants were asked to maintain their lifestyle, diet, medications, physical activity and sleep habits throughout the study.
All participants received written and verbal information and provided written informed consent before any study-related activity.

> Participants were phenotypically characterised (and intervention effects were assessed 20 ) by researcher-administered tests (Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) 21 ), self-administered questionnaires assessing mental health and sleep quality (Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS) 22, Perceived Stress Scale (PSS) 23, Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) 24, Gastrointestinal Symptom Rating Scale (GSRS) 25 ) and blood markers (high sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP), Supplementary Information 1).

> Block (size three and six) randomisation was performed, and participants were stratified by sex and age (born 1954 or later, born 1953 or earlier).

> Participants were instructed to consume the study product daily, together with breakfast, dissolved in 200 ml of cold or room temperature water or milk.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_exact.title: Exact P-Values
stat_p_exact.summary_text: We found 2 imprecise *p* values out of 2 detected *p* values.

table.formatted: FC of both with occipital pole/cortex and cerebellum, and of LC with pre-/postcentral gyrus, superior parietal lobule, insular/opercular cortex, putamen, and planum polare showed within-group changes (non-encapsulated), no between-group differences were observed (all p<0.0056).
table.expanded: FC of both with occipital pole/cortex and cerebellum, and of LC with pre-/postcentral gyrus, superior parietal lobule, insular/opercular cortex, putamen, and planum polare showed within-group changes (non-encapsulated), no between-group differences were observed (all p<0.0056).

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::
